10  Bar

How large is each category? bar draws a rectangle from the baseline (zero) to the value for each row. Bars are vertical when the categories are on x and horizontal when they are on y; see Horizontal bars.

The bar chart exists because William Playfair had too little data. His Commercial and Political Atlas of 1786 drew England’s imports and exports as two curves across thirty years (Playfair, 1786). For Scotland he had a single year, and no curve can show one year. So he drew a bar for each of Scotland’s trading partners instead, and wrote that the result was a weaker picture than a curve, because it showed no change over time. The form he apologized for became the one everyone knows.

Two names for it are still in use, and they name opposite orientations. Much of the business world, Excel included, calls this a column chart when the bars are vertical, and uses bar chart only when they are horizontal. gog has one bar, and its direction comes from whichever axis carries the category. A third name, histogram, belongs to a different plot drawn with the same mark. Karl Pearson introduced the word in the 1890s (Pearson, 1895) for the picture of a distribution. Its bars cover intervals cut from a continuous axis, and neighboring bars touch. In gog that plot is bar * bin, shown in Histogram below.

10.1 Basic usage

Which country won the most gold medals? Most examples in this chapter start from the smallest sentence that draws a bar: a source, the mark, and its two positions. The medals table holds one row for each of five countries, and each row gives the number of Olympic gold, silver and bronze medals that country won. The book’s data describes it and every other table in the book.

medals: all 5 rows
country gold silver bronze
USA 46 37 38
China 38 31 22
Great Britain 29 17 19
Russia 19 18 9
Germany 17 10 15
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold)
data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold)
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold)
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold))

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold.”

The x axis places a tick at each bar position automatically. The y axis reaches zero unless you state your own limits, so a bar’s length is its value.

10.2 Color

Every bar is the same color until you map a column to color. With a color for each bar, a reader can find one country quickly and match it to the same country in another plot, as long as that plot also colors by country. Bind color to the column that is already on x, and color fills each bar with a distinct color:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  color(country)
(data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  color(col.country))
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + color(:country)
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold), color(col.country))

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, color by country.”

The legend repeats the names on the x axis, because the same column is on both. color(country, legend = FALSE) keeps the colors and leaves the legend out.

10.3 Ordering bars

In what order should the bars appear? A reader looking for the largest value wants it first. A reader looking for one name wants the names in alphabetical order. order() controls the sequence of categories along whichever axis carries them: x on a vertical plot, y on a horizontal one. You can sort on the categorical column itself, on the measured column, or on a third column of numbers. After bar * count, you can also sort on the count. Naming the categorical column asks for that column’s own order. Here that is alphabetical, because order() sorts plain text such as country from A to Z. A column with a declared order uses that order instead.

Default, data order (rows as they appear in the table) is the order of the plot in Basic usage.

By value, descending, tallest bar first, the usual order for a ranking:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Gold medals: largest first")
(data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) +
  title("Gold medals: largest first"))
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + order(:gold, desc = true) +
  title("Gold medals: largest first")
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), title("Gold medals: largest first"))

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, largest first.”

These bars are in the same order as the plot in Basic usage. The medals table already lists the country with the most gold first, so ordering by gold changes nothing here. Writing the order anyway is still safer, because the plot then stays sorted even if next year’s table lists the countries in a different order. The plots below each put the bars in a different order.

By value, ascending, smallest first, useful when scanning for the lowest values:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold) +
  title("Gold medals: smallest first")
(data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold) +
  title("Gold medals: smallest first"))
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + order(:gold) +
  title("Gold medals: smallest first")
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold), order(col.gold),
  title("Gold medals: smallest first"))

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, smallest first.”

By category name, A → Z, natural for names and labels:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(country) +
  title("Gold medals: A to Z")
(data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.country) +
  title("Gold medals: A to Z"))
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + order(:country) +
  title("Gold medals: A to Z")
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold), order(col.country),
  title("Gold medals: A to Z"))

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by country, A to Z.”

By category name, Z → A, the reverse:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(country, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Gold medals: Z to A")
(data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.country, desc = True) +
  title("Gold medals: Z to A"))
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:country, desc = true) + title("Gold medals: Z to A")
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.country, { desc: true }), title("Gold medals: Z to A"))

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by country, Z to A.”

By a third column, order countries by their silver medal count, while plotting gold:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(silver, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Gold medals: ordered by silver")
(data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.silver, desc = True) +
  title("Gold medals: ordered by silver"))
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:silver, desc = true) + title("Gold medals: ordered by silver")
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.silver, { desc: true }),
  title("Gold medals: ordered by silver"))

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, ordered by silver, largest first.”

By the count, when each bar is a count of rows. The gapminder_2007 table holds one row for each of 142 countries in 2007. Each row gives the country’s continent, its life expectancy (life), its population and its GDP per person (gdp). The count transform, written bar * count, draws how many countries each continent has:

gapminder_2007: first 5 of 142 rows
country continent year life population gdp
Afghanistan Asia 2007 43.828 31889923 974.5803
Albania Europe 2007 76.423 3600523 5937.0295
Algeria Africa 2007 72.301 33333216 6223.3675
Angola Africa 2007 42.731 12420476 4797.2313
Argentina Americas 2007 75.320 40301927 12779.3796
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  order(count, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Countries per continent: largest first")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  order(col.count, desc = True) +
  title("Countries per continent: largest first"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  order(:count, desc = true) +
  title("Countries per continent: largest first")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  order(col.count, { desc: true }),
  title("Countries per continent: largest first"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, ordered by count, largest first.”

Africa, with 52 countries, comes first, and Oceania, with 2, comes last. The table has no count column. bar * count writes one, and order() names it like any other column of numbers. After bar * proportion, write order(proportion) in the same way. The Transforms chapter draws that plot.

Expression Order
(none) Data order (rows as they appear)
order(gold) Ascending by gold (smallest first)
order(gold, desc = TRUE) Descending by gold (largest first)
order(country) A → Z by country name
order(country, desc = TRUE) Z → A by country name
order(silver, desc = TRUE) By another column of numbers
order(count, desc = TRUE) Descending by the count that bar * count writes (largest first)

10.4 Duplicate categories

A table often holds several rows for one category, one per event or one per year. The question is still how large each category is in total. Without a transform, bar draws one bar per row, and rows that share a category share a slot. This table has two rows each for USA and GBR:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
medals_dup <- data.frame(
  country = c("USA", "USA", "GBR", "GBR", "JPN"),
  gold    = c(10, 5, 8, 4, 6)
)
data(medals_dup) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  title("Duplicate rows: no transform")
medals_dup = {
  "country": ["USA", "USA", "GBR", "GBR", "JPN"],
  "gold": [10, 5, 8, 4, 6],
}
(data(medals_dup) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  title("Duplicate rows: no transform"))
medals_dup = (
  country = ["USA", "USA", "GBR", "GBR", "JPN"],
  gold = [10, 5, 8, 4, 6],
)
data(medals_dup) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  title("Duplicate rows: no transform")
const medals_dup = {
  country: ["USA", "USA", "GBR", "GBR", "JPN"],
  gold: [10, 5, 8, 4, 6],
};
plot(data(medals_dup), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  title("Duplicate rows: no transform"))

“Given the medals dup table: bars, x is country, y is gold.”

Every bar grows from zero, so the shorter ones are drawn inside the tallest. USA has rows of 10 and 5, and its bar reads 10 rather than 15. Each bar is drawn slightly translucent, so the color is darker where two bars overlap. For USA, that darker band ends at 5, where the shorter bar stops. That band is the only sign that a category has extra rows. When two rows hold the same value, the two bars cover each other exactly. The whole bar is then darker than a bar of one row, and no band shows, so the darker color is the only sign.

Use the sum transform to total the values per category first:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) + title("Totals: bar * sum")
(data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) + title("Totals: bar * sum"))
data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:gold, desc = true) + title("Totals: bar * sum")
plot(data(medals_dup), layer(bar, sum), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), title("Totals: bar * sum"))

“Given the medals dup table: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, largest first.”

sum gives one number for each category. It reads every row that shares a category and totals them. USA’s 10 and 5 become 15, and GBR’s 8 and 4 become 12. Five rows become three bars, one for each country, and the darker band is gone.

count, from Ordering bars, also draws one bar for each category, but it measures something else. sum adds up the values in a column, here gold on y. count counts the rows in each category and reads no column. It writes its count on y itself, so y(gold) is refused (What it refuses). On this table it gives USA 2, GBR 2 and JPN 1, the number of rows for each country:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
   title("bar * sum + y(gold): gold added up")) |
  (data(medals_dup) + bar * count + x(country) +
     title("bar * count: rows counted"))
((data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
   title("bar * sum + y(gold): gold added up")) |
  (data(medals_dup) + bar * count + x(col.country) +
     title("bar * count: rows counted")))
(data(medals_dup) + bar * sum + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  title("bar * sum + y(gold): gold added up")) |
  (data(medals_dup) + bar * count + x(:country) +
  title("bar * count: rows counted"))
beside(plot(data(medals_dup), layer(bar, sum), x(col.country),
  y(col.gold), title("bar * sum + y(gold): gold added up")),
  plot(data(medals_dup), layer(bar, count), x(col.country),
  title("bar * count: rows counted")))

“Given the medals dup table: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold, beside bars derived by count, x is country.”

Use sum when you ask how much each category holds in total, such as gold medals or sales. Use count when you ask how many rows each category has, such as the countries of each continent.

10.5 Negative values

A bar can also point the other way, when a value is below zero, such as the profit of a quarter that lost money. Every bar starts at zero. That rule made the duplicate bars overlap, and it is also why a negative bar points down. So you write nothing extra for a negative value:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
balance <- data.frame(quarter = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"),
                      profit  = c(12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0))
data(balance) + bar + x(quarter) + y(profit) +
  title("Negative values grow downward from zero")
balance = {
  "quarter": ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  "profit": [12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0],
}
(data(balance) + bar + x(col.quarter) + y(col.profit) +
  title("Negative values grow downward from zero"))
balance = (
  quarter = ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  profit = [12, -5, 8, -2],
)
data(balance) + bar + x(:quarter) + y(:profit) +
  title("Negative values grow downward from zero")
const balance = {
  quarter: ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  profit: [12, -5, 8, -2],
};
plot(data(balance), bar, x(col.quarter), y(col.profit),
  title("Negative values grow downward from zero"))

“Given the balance table: bars, x is quarter, y is profit.”

To color the losses and the profits differently, you need a column that says which is which, because gog does not decide which bars are losses. Map that column with color, and let palette() say which colors the mapping uses. The table below sets the column’s values by hand. In practice you compute it from profit with one condition. Above zero is a profit, and anything else is a loss.

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
balance <- data.frame(
  quarter = c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"),
  profit  = c(12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0),
  result  = factor(c("profit", "loss", "profit", "loss"),
                   levels = c("loss", "profit"))
)
data(balance) + bar + x(quarter) + y(profit) + color(result) +
  palette(c("firebrick", "seagreen")) +
  title("Red below zero, green above")
import pandas as pd

balance = {
  "quarter": ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  "profit": [12.0, -5.0, 8.0, -2.0],
  "result": pd.Categorical(["profit", "loss", "profit", "loss"], categories=["loss", "profit"]),
}
(data(balance) + bar + x(col.quarter) + y(col.profit) + color(col.result) +
  palette(["firebrick", "seagreen"]) +
  title("Red below zero, green above"))
using CategoricalArrays
balance = (
  quarter = ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  profit = [12, -5, 8, -2],
  result = CategoricalArray(["profit", "loss", "profit", "loss"]; levels = ["loss", "profit"]),
)
data(balance) + bar + x(:quarter) + y(:profit) + color(:result) +
  palette(["firebrick", "seagreen"]) +
  title("Red below zero, green above")
const balance = {
  quarter: ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"],
  profit: [12, -5, 8, -2],
  result: ordered(["profit", "loss", "profit", "loss"], ["loss", "profit"]),
};
plot(data(balance), bar, x(col.quarter), y(col.profit), color(col.result),
  palette(["firebrick", "seagreen"]),
  title("Red below zero, green above"))

“Given the balance table: bars, x is quarter, y is profit, color by result, with a palette of firebrick and seagreen.”

palette() assigns its colors in category order, and that is why result carries a declared order here instead of being plain text. palette() does not sort plain text, and order() does not move its colors: it assigns them in the order the values first appear in the table. The first row here is a profit, so the palette would give firebrick to the profits. Declaring the order as loss, then profit, gives firebrick to the losses, and the legend lists them in that order. The colors then stay with their results, even if next year’s table starts with a loss. R spells that with a factor’s levels, Python with a pandas Categorical, Julia with a CategoricalArray, and JavaScript with ordered(). This is the same mechanism as Declaring the order of categories.

Red for loss and green for profit is one common convention. It is also the hardest pair to separate for red-green color blindness, the most common kind. Texture solves that and keeps the colors, by giving each result its own texture as well as its own color. Texture below draws these bars that way, and Will it read in gray? in the cookbook applies the same idea to other plots.

10.6 Horizontal bars

Sometimes the bars should be horizontal. The category names may be too long for the bottom axis. Or there may be many categories, and a tall list of horizontal bars reads more easily than a crowded row of vertical ones. Swap the bindings, and put the categories on y and the measure on x:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(gold) + y(country) +
  title("Categories on y: horizontal bars")
(data(medals) + bar + x(col.gold) + y(col.country) +
  title("Categories on y: horizontal bars"))
data(medals) + bar + x(:gold) + y(:country) +
  title("Categories on y: horizontal bars")
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.gold), y(col.country),
  title("Categories on y: horizontal bars"))

“Given the medals: bars, x is gold, y is country.”

If you know ggplot2’s coord_flip() or matplotlib’s barh(), gog has no such word, because it would be a second way to say one thing. gog takes the orientation from the bindings. The axis with the number is the one the bars grow along, so their length is read on it. The axis with the category is the one the bars are placed on, one slot each. Nothing else changes: order, transforms such as sum and bin, color and style() all behave as they do on vertical bars.

Horizontal bars help most when the category names are long. On a vertical axis each label is written across the page, so it does not have to fit inside one slot. The departments table holds the number of people (headcount) in each of five departments of one company. The department names are long:

departments: all 5 rows
department headcount
Research & Development 128
Sales and Marketing 96
Customer Operations 74
Finance 31
People & Culture 22
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(departments) + bar + x(headcount) + y(department) +
  order(headcount, desc = TRUE) +
  x_label("Headcount") +
  title("Long labels fit on a vertical axis")
(data(departments) + bar + x(col.headcount) + y(col.department) +
  order(col.headcount, desc = True) +
  x_label("Headcount") +
  title("Long labels fit on a vertical axis"))
data(departments) + bar + x(:headcount) + y(:department) +
  order(:headcount, desc = true) + x_label("Headcount") +
  title("Long labels fit on a vertical axis")
plot(data(departments), bar, x(col.headcount), y(col.department),
  order(col.headcount, { desc: true }), x_label("Headcount"),
  title("Long labels fit on a vertical axis"))

“Given the departments: bars, x is headcount, y is department, ordered by headcount, largest first.”

order means the same thing in both orientations: the first category in sort order takes the first slot. Descending puts the largest bar leftmost on a vertical plot and topmost on a horizontal one.

Only one pair of columns says nothing about orientation: two columns of plain numbers, such as year and sales. gog has one rule for that case: it measures the column on y and draws vertical bars. So x(year) + y(sales) gives vertical bars. Swapping the two bindings does not make the bars horizontal. x(sales) + y(year) also gives vertical bars. The quarterly table, despite its name, holds one sales figure for each year from 2005 to 2023. Both columns, year and sales, hold numbers:

quarterly: first 5 of 19 rows
year sales
2005 95
2006 104
2007 118
2008 112
2009 88
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(quarterly) + bar + x(year) + y(sales) + title("x(year) + y(sales)")) |
  (data(quarterly) + bar + x(sales) + y(year) + title("x(sales) + y(year)"))
((data(quarterly) + bar + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) + title("x(year) + y(sales)")) |
  (data(quarterly) + bar + x(col.sales) + y(col.year) + title("x(sales) + y(year)")))
(data(quarterly) + bar + x(:year) + y(:sales) +
  title("x(year) + y(sales)")) |
  (data(quarterly) + bar + x(:sales) + y(:year) +
  title("x(sales) + y(year)"))
beside(plot(data(quarterly), bar, x(col.year), y(col.sales),
  title("x(year) + y(sales)")),
  plot(data(quarterly), bar, x(col.sales), y(col.year),
  title("x(sales) + y(year)")))

“Given quarterly: bars, x is year, y is sales, beside bars, x is sales, y is year.”

Both plots draw vertical bars. On the left, each bar’s length is a year’s sales. On the right, each bar is drawn at its sales figure on x, and its length is its year. Every year is about 2,000, which the axis writes as 2K, so all the bars look the same height. A year is not an amount, so these lengths measure nothing.

For horizontal bars, make the year categorical and put it on y. A column of numbers becomes categorical when you declare the order of its values. Each year then gets a slot of its own, and the bars grow along x. The gm_eras table holds 284 rows: one for each of 142 countries in 1957, and again in 2007. It stores the year twice. year holds it as a number, and era holds the same year as a category, made from year by declaring the order of its values:

gm_eras: first 5 of 284 rows
country continent year life population gdp era
Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.332 9240934 820.8530 1957
Afghanistan Asia 2007 43.828 31889923 974.5803 2007
Albania Europe 1957 59.280 1476505 1942.2842 1957
Albania Europe 2007 76.423 3600523 5937.0295 2007
Algeria Africa 1957 45.685 10270856 3013.9760 1957

Each year has 142 rows, one for each country, so mean averages their life expectancies into one bar for each year:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(life) + y(era) +
  x_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("era on y: horizontal bars")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(col.life) + y(col.era) +
  x_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("era on y: horizontal bars"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(:life) + y(:era) +
  x_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("era on y: horizontal bars")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean), x(col.life), y(col.era),
  x_label("Mean life expectancy"), title("era on y: horizontal bars"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean, x is life, y is era.”

The two bars grow along x: the mean life expectancy was about 52 years in 1957 and about 67 in 2007.

A column of dates needs no such step. A bar never measures a date, so dates on y make the bars horizontal, as Bars on a date axis shows.

A bar needs something to measure, so two categorical axes are refused. What it refuses shows that refusal.

10.7 Texture

The profit and loss bars in Negative values are red and green, the pair hardest to distinguish for a reader with red-green color blindness. Give each result its own texture as well, and that reader can separate the bars without seeing color at all.

A bar’s fill can carry a texture: lines or dots repeated across the bar, in the bar’s color. You set it with style(pattern = ). A texture does not need color, so a hatched bar chart stays legible in grayscale or in a black-and-white print:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) +
  style(pattern = "hatch") +
  title("A hatched bar reads without color")
(data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  style(pattern = "hatch") +
  title("A hatched bar reads without color"))
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + style(pattern = "hatch") +
  title("A hatched bar reads without color")
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  style({ pattern: "hatch" }), title("A hatched bar reads without color"))

“Given the medals: bars, x is country, y is gold, with pattern hatch.”

style(pattern = ) gives every bar in the layer the same texture. To give each category its own texture, map a column with the pattern() channel, which does for texture what shape() does for glyphs. The plot below maps the texture column with pattern(). Each bar then shows one of the six fill textures, in this order: "solid" (the default, a plain fill), "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid" and "dots":

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
textures <- data.frame(
  texture = c("solid", "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots"),
  height  = c(6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1)
)
data(textures) + bar + x(texture) + y(height) + pattern(texture) +
  x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The six fill textures")
textures = {
  "texture": ["solid", "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots"],
  "height": [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1],
}
(data(textures) + bar + x(col.texture) + y(col.height) + pattern(col.texture) +
  x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The six fill textures"))
textures = (
  texture = ["solid", "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots"],
  height = [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1],
)
data(textures) + bar + x(:texture) + y(:height) + pattern(:texture) +
  x_label("") + y_label("") + title("The six fill textures")
const textures = {
  texture: ["solid", "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots"],
  height: [6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1],
};
plot(data(textures), bar, x(col.texture), y(col.height),
  pattern(col.texture), x_label(""), y_label(""),
  title("The six fill textures"))

“Given the textures table: bars, x is texture, y is height, pattern by texture.”

With more than six categories, the textures repeat: a seventh category gets "solid" again. gog prints a message when that happens, and it suggests color(), whose default palette has twenty colors, or facet().

The style chapter shows them beside the stroke patterns a line takes, because style(pattern = ) is one name whose values depend on the shape: fill textures on a fill, stroke patterns on a stroke.

For the profit and loss bars, write pattern(result) beside color(result). The plot below uses the balance table from Negative values:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(balance) + bar + x(quarter) + y(profit) + color(result) +
  pattern(result) + palette(c("firebrick", "seagreen")) +
  title("A color and a texture for each result")
(data(balance) + bar + x(col.quarter) + y(col.profit) + color(col.result) +
  pattern(col.result) + palette(["firebrick", "seagreen"]) +
  title("A color and a texture for each result"))
data(balance) + bar + x(:quarter) + y(:profit) + color(:result) +
  pattern(:result) + palette(["firebrick", "seagreen"]) +
  title("A color and a texture for each result")
plot(data(balance), bar, x(col.quarter), y(col.profit), color(col.result),
  pattern(col.result), palette(["firebrick", "seagreen"]),
  title("A color and a texture for each result"))

“Given the balance table: bars, x is quarter, y is profit, color by result, pattern by result, with a palette of firebrick and seagreen.”

The losses stay solid and the profits are hatched, so each result has its own color and its own texture. Both channels read the same column, so one legend shows both. A reader who cannot tell the red from the green can still tell the solid bars from the hatched ones.

10.8 Histogram

How are the world’s life expectancies spread out, and where do most countries fall? That is a question about one continuous column. To answer it, each bar has to count the rows whose values fall in one range of that column. The bin transform makes those ranges: it cuts the x axis into equal-width intervals, called bins, and counts the rows in each. The gapminder_2007 table, shown in Ordering bars, holds one life expectancy for each of 142 countries. Combine bar with bin to create a histogram:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) + y(count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) + y(col.count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) + y(:count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life), y(col.count),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), y_label("Count"),
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life, y is count.”

gapminder_2007 has no count column. bin writes the counts into a new column named count, and y(count) refers to it. count is the only name y() takes here. To label the axis in your own words, use y_label() (The name on a measure axis).

A bar’s width is automatic, and it is the clearest way a histogram and a bar chart differ on the page. A categorical bar fills 80% of its slot, which leaves a gap between neighboring bars. That gap is what reads as separate categories. A histogram cuts a continuous axis into adjacent intervals, so there is no space between one bin and the next, and the bars touch. A thin line in the panel’s background color is drawn between neighboring bars, so each one can still be seen. In both kinds of plot, the gold medal chart in Basic usage and this histogram, gog takes the bar’s width from the axis, so you set nothing.

A bar can also be drawn on a continuous axis without bin. Its slot is then the smallest distance between two neighboring values. Two countries here differ in GDP by less than a dollar, so the slot is narrower than a pixel. gog then draws every bar one pixel wide, at its own value:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  title("Bars on a continuous axis, without bin")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  title("Bars on a continuous axis, without bin"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  title("Bars on a continuous axis, without bin")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), bar, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  title("Bars on a continuous axis, without bin"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars, x is gdp, y is life.”

Each bar is one country. Where many countries have a similar GDP, the bars touch and form one solid block. To see how the values spread, cut the axis into bins with bin. To read each country’s position, draw point.

bin is not only for bars. Four other marks can draw the same bins, and only the shape changes:

Mark derived by bin Shape
point * bin one dot at the top of each bin
line * bin the frequency polygon: straight lines through the bin centers
area * bin the same polygon, filled to the baseline
step * bin the staircase outline, drawn in Step
bar * bin filled bars, the histogram above

zone * bin and surface * bin cut two axes instead of one: the heatmap in Zone and the sheet in Surface.

The width of each bin decides what the histogram shows. With no argument, bin picks the number of bins from the number of rows, by Sturges’ rule (Sturges, 1926). The rule is simple: each time the number of rows doubles, the histogram gets one more bin. So 100 rows get 8 bins, the 142 countries here get 9, and 1,000 rows get 11. Write a width with its name, width =, to cut the axis in the column’s own units. A number without a name always sets how many bins there are, so bin(5) means five bins, not five years. Below, bin(width = 5) cuts the axis into bins five years wide, and bin(30) into thirty bins:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(life) + y(count) +
   x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
   title("bin(width = 5): bins five years wide")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(life) + y(count) +
     x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
     title("bin(30): thirty bins"))
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(col.life) + y(col.count) +
   x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
   title("bin(width = 5): bins five years wide")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(col.life) + y(col.count) +
     x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
     title("bin(30): thirty bins")))
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(:life) + y(:count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("bin(width = 5): bins five years wide")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(:life) + y(:count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("bin(30): thirty bins"))
beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin({ width: 5 })),
  x(col.life), y(col.count), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  y_label("Count"), title("bin(width = 5): bins five years wide")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin(30)), x(col.life),
  y(col.count), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), y_label("Count"),
  title("bin(30): thirty bins")))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin at width 5, x is life, y is count, beside bars derived by bin into 30, x is life, y is count.”

Five-year bins give ten bars, and the shape is easy to read. Nearly half of the countries, 70 of 142, fall between 70 and 80 years, and 39 of them between 70 and 75. Thirty bins are each about 1.4 years wide, so the counts are smaller and change more from one bar to the next. One bin, from about 68.3 to 69.7 years, holds no country, so 29 bars are drawn, with a gap the five-year bins hide. Both plots write y(count), so they share one count axis (A column two plots share), and the heights compare directly: the tallest bar on the right holds 15 countries, and the tallest on the left holds 39.

Use a width when each bin should cover a span that means something, such as five years. Use a number of bins when you only want more detail or less. Choosing the bin count explains why a number without a name always means bins, and why gog refuses both at once. Choosing a width explains how to pick a width for your own column.

A histogram can also be horizontal, by the rule in Horizontal bars. Bind the column you are binning to y, and the count is drawn along x. The sentence does not have to name the count: bin computes it and draws it on the other axis, so y(count) in the first histogram was optional:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same histogram, horizontal")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same histogram, horizontal"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same histogram, horizontal")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("The same histogram, horizontal"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, y is life.”

10.8.1 Where the bin edges fall

This section reads the edges of the five-year histogram from Histogram, so it is drawn again here:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(life) + y(count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Bins five years wide")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(col.life) + y(col.count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Bins five years wide"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(:life) + y(:count) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + y_label("Count") +
  title("Bins five years wide")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin({ width: 5 })), x(col.life),
  y(col.count), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), y_label("Count"),
  title("Bins five years wide"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin at width 5, x is life, y is count.”

Its first bin starts at 35, although the shortest life expectancy in the table is 39.6. An edge is a value where one bin ends and the next begins, and where the edges fall is a choice. Each bar counts the rows between its two edges, such as the countries with a life expectancy from 40 to 45. Suppose every edge were 2.5 years higher: the bins would run from 37.5 to 42.5, from 42.5 to 47.5, and so on. A country at 41 years would then be counted in the bin from 37.5 to 42.5, not in the bin from 40 to 45. When countries change bins, the counts change, and the shape of the histogram can change with them.

When you name a width, gog makes every edge a multiple of that width. The first bin is the one that holds the smallest value. For these countries, the five-year bins therefore run from 35 to 40, from 40 to 45, and so on up to 85. In the plot above, every gridline from 40 to 80 is also a bin edge. A value exactly on an edge is counted in the bin that starts there, so a life expectancy of 40 belongs to the bin from 40 to 45.

Edges on multiples of the width come from Leland Wilkinson’s The Grammar of Graphics, the book that gog is named after (Wilkinson, 2005). He advises one edge at zero. Every edge is then a multiple of the width, a round number that a reader can find on the axis. He also says it should not be a strict rule, because the edges change the shape of the histogram. Round edges are easy to read, but other edges can give a smoother shape.

Wilkinson also treats one kind of column separately: a column that holds only a few distinct values, such as the whole numbers from 0 to 10. With bins one unit wide, every value of such a column falls exactly on an edge. The bar for 3 is then drawn from 3 to 4, not centered on 3. He gives each possible value a bin of its own instead, centered on that value. In gog the nearest sentence is bar * count, with one difference: it gives a slot to each value that occurs, not to each possible value. Each bar is centered on its value. The width of each slot is the smallest distance between two values that occur. A column that holds only 3 and 7 therefore gets two wide bars side by side, with no empty slot between them. A column that holds 3, 4, 6 and 7 gets slots one unit wide, and the slot for 5, a value that never occurs, is left empty. Below, bar * bin(width = 1) and bar * count draw the same seven scores. The score 3 occurs once, 4 twice, 6 three times and 7 once:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
scores <- data.frame(score = c(3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7))
(data(scores) + bar * bin(width = 1) + x(score) + title("bar * bin(width = 1)")) |
  (data(scores) + bar * count + x(score) + title("bar * count"))
scores = {"score": [3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7]}
((data(scores) + bar * bin(width = 1) + x(col.score) + title("bar * bin(width = 1)")) |
  (data(scores) + bar * count + x(col.score) + title("bar * count")))
scores = (score = [3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7],)
(data(scores) + bar * bin(width = 1) + x(:score) +
  title("bar * bin(width = 1)")) |
  (data(scores) + bar * count + x(:score) + title("bar * count"))
const scores = { score: [3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 6, 7] };
beside(plot(data(scores), layer(bar, bin({ width: 1 })), x(col.score),
  title("bar * bin(width = 1)")),
  plot(data(scores), layer(bar, count), x(col.score),
  title("bar * count")))

“Given the scores table: bars derived by bin at width 1, x is score, beside bars derived by count, x is score.”

On the left, each bar starts at its value. The bar for 3 runs from 3 to 4, so the tick for 3 is at its left end, and a reader can take that bar for a score of 3.5. On the right, each bar is centered on its value. No score is 5, so the bin from 5 to 6 on the left is empty, and so is the slot for 5 on the right, which has no tick. The left axis reaches 8 because the bin for 7 ends there. For a column of a few whole numbers, use bar * count.

When you give the number of bins instead of a width, the edges are placed differently. bin(30) divides the range from the smallest value to the largest into thirty equal bins. For the 142 life expectancies, each bin is 1.43 years wide, as in the bin(30) plot in Histogram, so the edges are not round numbers. For round edges, name a width instead. With no argument, bin chooses the number of bins itself, by Sturges’ rule, so its edges also run from the smallest value to the largest.

ggplot2 places its edges differently (Wickham et al., 2026). Given a width, ggplot2 puts the center of a bin at zero, where gog puts an edge. Its five-year bins therefore run from 37.5 to 42.5, from 42.5 to 47.5, and so on. Given the number of bins, ggplot2 makes each bin slightly wider than gog does. Its first bin is then centered on the smallest value, and its last on the largest. In ggplot2, a value exactly on an edge goes to the bin that ends there. Both packages count every row once, but the bins cover different years, so the shapes differ. On this table, gog’s last five-year bin, 80 to 85, holds 13 countries, while ggplot2’s, 82.5 to 87.5, holds only Japan.

To put the edges anywhere else, state where the axis starts, and the first bin starts there too. x(life, limits = c(37.5, 87.5)) gives the five-year edges that ggplot2 uses. Scales explains limits.

10.8.2 Overlaid histograms: one distribution per group

The iris flowers table holds measurements of 150 flowers from three species. A single histogram of all the flowers answers “how is petal length distributed?” It cannot answer “how is it distributed for each species?” Add color and the histogram splits: one histogram per category, cut on the same bins and drawn in the same panel.

iris_flowers: first 5 of 150 rows
sepal_length sepal_width petal_length species
5.1 3.5 1.4 setosa
4.9 3.0 1.4 setosa
4.7 3.2 1.3 setosa
4.6 3.1 1.5 setosa
5.0 3.6 1.4 setosa
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Petal length by species")
(data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(col.petal_length) + color(col.species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Petal length by species"))
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(:petal_length) + color(:species) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Petal length by species")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(bar, bin), x(col.petal_length),
  color(col.species), x_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Petal length by species"))

“Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by species.”

The three histograms overlay. None of them is moved aside, and all three measure from the same baseline. If the fills were opaque, the species drawn last would hide the others wherever they overlap. So each bar is a translucent fill under a solid outline in its own color. The outline is what keeps the shape readable where the fills overlap. setosa is alone on the left and reads clearly. versicolor and virginica overlap in the middle, and their outlines still separate them. The groups share the same bins, so their bars align, and an overlap in the plot is an overlap in the data.

style(opacity = ) sets how faint the fill is; the outline stays solid whatever you choose:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A heavier fill: style(opacity = 0.6)")
(data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(col.petal_length) + color(col.species) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A heavier fill: style(opacity = 0.6)"))
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(:petal_length) + color(:species) +
  style(opacity = 0.6) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("A heavier fill: style(opacity = 0.6)")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(bar, bin), x(col.petal_length),
  color(col.species), style({ opacity: 0.6 }),
  x_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("A heavier fill: style(opacity = 0.6)"))

“Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by species, with opacity 0.6.”

The outline is the group’s color by default, but you can recolor it: style(border_color = ) sets the border, style(border_size = ) its width. A black border separates the overlapping fills, the way many overlaid histograms are drawn. It also stays visible against the light panel, where a white one disappears:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  style(border_color = "black", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Black borders between the fills")
(data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(col.petal_length) + color(col.species) +
  style(border_color = "black", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Black borders between the fills"))
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(:petal_length) + color(:species) +
  style(border_color = "black", border_size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("Black borders between the fills")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(bar, bin), x(col.petal_length),
  color(col.species), style({ border_color: "black", border_size: 1.5 }),
  x_label("Petal length (cm)"), title("Black borders between the fills"))

“Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by species, with border color black and border size 1.5.”

The fill and the outline are independent: a bar can be one color inside and another at its edge, whether the fill was mapped (as here) or set. See Setting vs mapping.

Or remove the outline entirely. style(border_size = 0) draws no border, so the translucent fills overlap with nothing between them. This is the plainest overlaid histogram:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(petal_length) + color(species) +
  style(border_size = 0) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("No border: just the fills")
(data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(col.petal_length) + color(col.species) +
  style(border_size = 0) +
  x_label("Petal length (cm)") + title("No border: just the fills"))
data(iris_flowers) + bar * bin + x(:petal_length) + color(:species) +
  style(border_size = 0) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("No border: just the fills")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(bar, bin), x(col.petal_length),
  color(col.species), style({ border_size: 0 }),
  x_label("Petal length (cm)"), title("No border: just the fills"))

“Given the iris flowers: bars derived by bin, x is petal length, color by species, with border size 0.”

When the groups overlap so much that the outlines are hard to distinguish, give each species its own panel instead. Adding | facet(species) to the sentence draws the same three histograms side by side, on one shared scale. Or draw one smooth curve per species, as in Area. A curve has no bins, so two species that overlap show as two lines that cross, not as two sets of bars drawn over each other.

10.8.3 The cumulative histogram

A histogram’s bar counts the rows in one bin. Add cumulative, and each bar counts the rows in its bin and in every bin to its left. Each bar still grows from zero, so its height is the total so far:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("bar * bin * cumulative: the cumulative histogram")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("bar * bin * cumulative: the cumulative histogram"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("bar * bin * cumulative: the cumulative histogram")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin, cumulative), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("bar * bin * cumulative: the cumulative histogram"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and cumulative, x is life.”

The last bar is 142, every country in the table. Each bar is taller than the one before it by the count of its own bin. The three largest rises, between about 68 and 83 years, come from the three bins that hold the most countries. The axis is labeled “Cumulative”, because each bar is a running total, not the count of one bin.

10.9 A waterfall: each bar from the previous total

A waterfall chart shows how each item in a list adds to a total or takes from it, one item after another. In finance, the most common one is drawn from an income statement: a company’s revenue, and the costs taken from it one by one. Each item is a bar that starts at the total before it, so the bar’s length is the item’s own amount. bar * cumulative adds up the same running total, but each of its bars starts at zero. cumulative(start_from = "previous") starts each bar at the total before it instead.

The income table is an invented income statement, with one row for each item. amount holds each item’s own number, and a cost is negative:

income: all 6 rows
item amount
Revenue 500
Cost of goods -290
Operating costs -130
Interest -10
Other income 15
Tax -20
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(income) + x(item) + y(amount) +
  bar * cumulative(start_from = "previous", total = TRUE) +
  color(direction) + palette(c("seagreen", "indianred", "steelblue")) +
  text * cumulative(start_from = "previous", total = TRUE) + label(amount) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("") + y_label("Amount (thousands)") +
  title("From revenue to net income")
(data(income) + x(col.item) + y(col.amount) +
  bar * cumulative(start_from = "previous", total = True) +
  color(col.direction) + palette(["seagreen", "indianred", "steelblue"]) +
  text * cumulative(start_from = "previous", total = True) + label(col.amount) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("") + y_label("Amount (thousands)") +
  title("From revenue to net income"))
data(income) + x(:item) + y(:amount) +
  bar * cumulative(start_from = "previous", total = true) +
  color(:direction) + palette(["seagreen", "indianred", "steelblue"]) +
  text * cumulative(start_from = "previous", total = true) +
  label(:amount) + style(nudge = "up") + x_label("") +
  y_label("Amount (thousands)") + title("From revenue to net income")
plot(data(income), x(col.item), y(col.amount),
  layer(bar, cumulative({ start_from: "previous", total: true })),
  color(col.direction), palette(["seagreen", "indianred", "steelblue"]),
  layer(text, cumulative({ start_from: "previous", total: true })),
  label(col.amount), style({ nudge: "up" }), x_label(""),
  y_label("Amount (thousands)"), title("From revenue to net income"))

“Given the income table: x is item, y is amount, bars derived by cumulative starting from the previous total, with a closing total, colored by direction, with a palette of seagreen, indianred and steelblue, and also text derived by cumulative starting from the previous total, with a closing total, label by amount, with nudge up.”

Read it from the left. Revenue is 500 thousand. The cost of goods takes 290 of it, so its bar runs from 500 down to 210, the gross profit. Operating costs take 130 more, down to 80, the operating income. Interest takes 10, other income adds 15, and tax takes 20, which leaves a net income of 65. The last bar is the closing bar, in a category named total. total = TRUE adds it after the last item and draws it from zero to the final running total, the net income of 65. No column of the table holds 210, 80 or 65. They are the running totals after the cost of goods, the operating costs and the tax, and cumulative computes them. The income table declares the order of item as the order of the statement, and cumulative adds the items up in that order.

cumulative also writes a column of its own, direction. It holds increase where an item adds to the total, decrease where an item takes from the total, and total for the closing bar. color(direction) colors the bars by it, and the palette gives the three colors in that order: green, red and blue. The second layer prints each item’s amount at the middle of its bar, and the final running total, 65, on the closing bar. style(nudge = "up") moves each label up a little, so the labels of the three short bars (interest, other income and tax) are drawn just above them.

Long item names are easier to read down the side of the plot. With y(item) and x(amount), the same bars run across the page, with the first item at the top. The plot below also changes the three colors. palette() takes any three colors you choose, and gives them to increase, decrease and total, in that order. Green and red are hard to distinguish for a reader with red-green color blindness. Blue and orange are easy to distinguish. This plot uses blue for an increase, orange for a decrease and gray for the closing bar:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(income) + bar * cumulative(start_from = "previous", total = TRUE) +
  y(item) + x(amount) +
  color(direction) + palette(c("steelblue", "darkorange", "slategray")) +
  y_label("") + x_label("Amount (thousands)") +
  title("From revenue to net income, across the page")
(data(income) + bar * cumulative(start_from = "previous", total = True) +
  y(col.item) + x(col.amount) +
  color(col.direction) + palette(["steelblue", "darkorange", "slategray"]) +
  y_label("") + x_label("Amount (thousands)") +
  title("From revenue to net income, across the page"))
data(income) + bar * cumulative(start_from = "previous", total = true) +
  y(:item) + x(:amount) + color(:direction) +
  palette(["steelblue", "darkorange", "slategray"]) + y_label("") +
  x_label("Amount (thousands)") +
  title("From revenue to net income, across the page")
plot(data(income),
  layer(bar, cumulative({ start_from: "previous", total: true })),
  y(col.item), x(col.amount), color(col.direction),
  palette(["steelblue", "darkorange", "slategray"]), y_label(""),
  x_label("Amount (thousands)"),
  title("From revenue to net income, across the page"))

“Given the income table: bars derived by cumulative starting from the previous total, with a closing total, y is item, x is amount, color by direction, with a palette of steelblue, darkorange and slategray.”

10.10 Grouped bars: side by side

How did each continent’s life expectancy change between 1957 and 2007? That is a comparison inside each category, so each continent needs two bars, one per era. A color split alone draws both bars in one slot, the shorter inside the taller. To set them side by side as a grouped bar chart, add dodge. Each group’s bar narrows to share the slot, and the split reads as a comparison within each category. The gm_eras table, shown in Horizontal bars, holds the two years 1957 and 2007. mean averages the countries into one value for each continent and era. era is the column that splits each continent into two bars.

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”

dodge is a collision modifier: it moves the bars rather than summarizing them, so it composes with the statistic (bar * mean * dodge here, bar * count * dodge for tallies). See Transforms for all four collision modifiers. A text layer over dodged bars takes the same dodge and a split of its own, such as group(era), so each number is printed on its own bar (Labels on dodged bars).

mean is the right statistic here, and gog will not choose it for you. Write sum in its place and gog still draws it:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  y_label("Sum of life expectancies") +
  title("Sum in place of mean: legal, and meaningless")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
  y_label("Sum of life expectancies") +
  title("Sum in place of mean: legal, and meaningless"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + y_label("Sum of life expectancies") +
  title("Sum in place of mean: legal, and meaningless")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, sum, dodge), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  color(col.era), y_label("Sum of life expectancies"),
  title("Sum in place of mean: legal, and meaningless"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by sum and dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”

Africa’s fifty-two life expectancies for 2007 are added into one bar of 2,850 years. A sum of life expectancies has no meaning. You may write either statistic. Which one is meaningful depends on what the column measures, and Law 8 says why gog leaves that choice to you.

10.10.1 The gap beside each bar

In a grouped bar chart, the two bars of each continent do not touch, as the second plot below shows. The pair is given the width of one bar, and each bar an equal part of it. Two bars that touch can read as one wide bar, so each bar leaves a fifth of its part empty. style(gap = ) sets that share, from 0, where the bars touch, to just under 1, where almost nothing remains to draw. If you do not set it, the gap is 0.2, a fifth. The four plots below set it to 0, leave it unset, and set it to 0.5 and 0.9:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
    style(gap = 0) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
    title("gap = 0: the two bars of a continent touch")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
      y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("gap unset: 0.2, the default")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
      style(gap = 0.5) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
      title("gap = 0.5: each bar half as wide as its part")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
      style(gap = 0.9) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
      title("gap = 0.9: each bar a tenth as wide as its part"))) +
  theme(height = 1150)
(((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
    style(gap = 0) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
    title("gap = 0: the two bars of a continent touch")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
      y_label("Mean life expectancy") + title("gap unset: 0.2, the default")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
      style(gap = 0.5) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
      title("gap = 0.5: each bar half as wide as its part")) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
      style(gap = 0.9) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
      title("gap = 0.9: each bar a tenth as wide as its part"))) +
  theme(height = 1150))
((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + style(gap = 0) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("gap = 0: the two bars of a continent touch")) /
  (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("gap unset: 0.2, the default")) /
  (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + style(gap = 0.5) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("gap = 0.5: each bar half as wide as its part")) /
  (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + style(gap = 0.9) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("gap = 0.9: each bar a tenth as wide as its part"))) +
  theme(height = 1150)
below(below(below(plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge),
  x(col.continent), y(col.life), color(col.era), style({ gap: 0 }),
  y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("gap = 0: the two bars of a continent touch")),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("gap unset: 0.2, the default"))),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), style({ gap: 0.5 }),
  y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("gap = 0.5: each bar half as wide as its part"))),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), style({ gap: 0.9 }),
  y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("gap = 0.9: each bar a tenth as wide as its part")),
  theme({ height: 1150 }))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era, with gap 0, above bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era, above the same with gap 0.5, above the same with gap 0.9.”

With gap 0, the two bars of each continent touch. With 0.5, each bar is half as wide as its part, and with 0.9, each bar is a tenth as wide as its part. On dodged bars, gap acts only inside each bar’s part, so in all four plots each bar stays at the center of its part. A larger gap narrows each bar from both sides, and the space between continents grows with it. The gap matters most when the two bars share one color and differ only in their pattern.

The gap must be less than 1. At 1 nothing would be left to draw, so gog refuses the sentence:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  style(gap = 1)
(data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
  style(gap = 1))
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + style(gap = 1)
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), style({ gap: 1 }))
Error:
! gog: `style(gap = 1)` is outside 0 to 1. It is the share of each bar's slot left empty, or of its part of the slot when it is dodged: 0 makes neighbors touch, and 0.5 leaves half. At 1 nothing would be left to draw.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

On a bar that is not dodged, gap is a share of the whole slot, and the default is again a fifth. style(gap = 0.5) leaves half of each slot empty, so each bar is half as wide as its slot. A histogram’s bars leave no gap unless you set one, because its bins are intervals that meet.

10.10.2 Splitting without color

The plots below show each continent’s mean life expectancy in 1957 and 2007 as bars. An error bar on each bar shows the 95% confidence interval of its mean. A second layer, interval * confidence(0.95), draws the error bars (Interval).

Bars with error bars are usually drawn in one of two ways. In the first, each era’s bars have their own color, and the error bars are black. In the second, the bars are gray, and each era’s error bars have their own color. The first is more common, but neither is wrong. The choice is a matter of taste. Neither way colors both layers by era. If it did, the part of each error bar below the mean would be drawn on a bar of the same color and be hard to see.

In both ways, each era needs its own bar and its own error bar, so the layer in one color still needs group(era). color(era) does two things at once: it splits each continent’s rows by era, and it paints each era its own color. group(era) does only the first. Without it, dodge in that layer has no groups to set side by side, and gog refuses the sentence. So the layer with the colors takes color(era), and the layer in one color takes group(era) and style(color = ). A channel such as color or group, written after a mark, reaches only the nearest mark before it, so each layer has its own. x and y are positions, which every layer shares, so writing them last changes nothing (Which marks a channel reaches):

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(gm_eras) +
   bar * mean * dodge + color(era) +
   interval * confidence(0.95) * dodge + group(era) +
   style(center = FALSE, color = "black") +
   x(continent) + y(life) + y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)") +
   title("Colored bars, black error bars")) /
  (data(gm_eras) +
     bar * mean * dodge + group(era) + style(color = "lightgray") +
     interval * confidence(0.95) * dodge + color(era) + style(center = FALSE) +
     x(continent) + y(life) + y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)") +
     title("Gray bars, colored error bars")) +
  theme(height = 900)
((data(gm_eras) +
   bar * mean * dodge + color(col.era) +
   interval * confidence(0.95) * dodge + group(col.era) +
   style(center = False, color = "black") +
   x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)") +
   title("Colored bars, black error bars")) /
  (data(gm_eras) +
     bar * mean * dodge + group(col.era) + style(color = "lightgray") +
     interval * confidence(0.95) * dodge + color(col.era) + style(center = False) +
     x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)") +
     title("Gray bars, colored error bars")) +
  theme(height = 900))
(data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + color(:era) +
  interval * confidence(0.95) * dodge + group(:era) +
  style(center = false, color = "black") + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Colored bars, black error bars")) /
  (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + group(:era) +
  style(color = "lightgray") + interval * confidence(0.95) * dodge +
  color(:era) + style(center = false) + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Gray bars, colored error bars")) + theme(height = 900)
below(plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), color(col.era),
  layer(interval, confidence(0.95), dodge), group(col.era),
  style({ center: false, color: "black" }), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Colored bars, black error bars")),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), group(col.era),
  style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(interval, confidence(0.95), dodge),
  color(col.era), style({ center: false }), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  y_label("Mean life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Gray bars, colored error bars")), theme({ height: 900 }))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, colored by era, and also intervals derived by confidence at 95% and dodge, grouped by era, with center off, colored black, x is continent, y is life, above bars derived by mean and dodge, grouped by era, colored lightgray, and also intervals derived by confidence at 95% and dodge, colored by era, with center off, x is continent, y is life.”

style(center = FALSE) leaves out each error bar’s center dot, because the bar already marks the mean. In the upper plot, the black error bars are clear on both colors, below the mean as well as above it.

A bar takes group only when a statistic, dodge or stack acts on its rows. With group(era), a statistic such as mean computes one value for each era in a slot, not one for the whole slot. dodge sets each era’s bar beside the others, and stack sets it on top of them (Stacked bars, below). With none of these, gog refuses group (What it refuses). The four plots below show why. They draw the same table on the same axes and differ in their transform. The top-left plot, with no transform, also has no group(era), because gog refuses it there:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
((data(gm_eras) + bar + x(continent) + y(life) + title("bar: one bar per row")) |
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + group(era) +
      title("bar * dodge: eras apart, countries overlap"))) /
  ((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) + group(era) +
      title("bar * mean: two means, one slot")) |
     (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + group(era) +
        title("bar * mean * dodge: two means, side by side"))) +
  theme(height = 750)
(((data(gm_eras) + bar + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + title("bar: one bar per row")) |
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + group(col.era) +
      title("bar * dodge: eras apart, countries overlap"))) /
  ((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + group(col.era) +
      title("bar * mean: two means, one slot")) |
     (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + group(col.era) +
        title("bar * mean * dodge: two means, side by side"))) +
  theme(height = 750))
((data(gm_eras) + bar + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  title("bar: one bar per row")) |
  (data(gm_eras) + bar * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) + group(:era) +
  title("bar * dodge: eras apart, countries overlap"))) /
  ((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) + group(:era) +
  title("bar * mean: two means, one slot")) |
  (data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  group(:era) + title("bar * mean * dodge: two means, side by side"))) +
  theme(height = 750)
below(beside(plot(data(gm_eras), bar, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  title("bar: one bar per row")),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, dodge), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  group(col.era), title("bar * dodge: eras apart, countries overlap"))),
  beside(plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), group(col.era), title("bar * mean: two means, one slot")),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), group(col.era),
  title("bar * mean * dodge: two means, side by side"))),
  theme({ height: 750 }))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars, x is continent, y is life, beside bars derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life, grouped by era; above bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, grouped by era, beside bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, grouped by era.”

With no transform, gog draws one bar for each row. The 284 rows of gm_eras become 284 bars, and the bars of one continent overlap in one slot, the shorter ones inside the tallest. Only the tallest bar in each slot can be seen, so the plot shows each continent’s longest life expectancy, as in Duplicate categories. Where a bar goes depends only on its continent, not on its era, so group(era) would leave this plot exactly as it is. With dodge and no statistic, the two eras’ bars are set side by side, but each side still holds one bar per country, the shorter ones inside the tallest. With mean and no dodge, each era gets one bar, but the two share one slot. Each bar is slightly translucent, so in each slot the color is darker where the 1957 bar and the taller 2007 bar overlap. With mean * dodge, each era gets one bar, and the two are drawn side by side. In both dodged plots, the left bar of each slot is 1957 and the right bar is 2007.

A stack can be split by group too, when each bar’s total matters more than its segments. Every segment then has the same color, so gog separates them with a thin line in the panel’s background color. It is the line that separates the bars of a histogram. The channel_sales table holds each quarter’s revenue from two ways of selling. Its channel column names them, Retail and Online. The table has one row for each quarter and way of selling, so stack needs no statistic:

channel_sales: first 5 of 6 rows
quarter channel revenue
Q1 Retail 4
Q1 Online 3
Q2 Retail 5
Q2 Online 6
Q3 Retail 4
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(channel_sales) + bar * stack + x(quarter) + y(revenue) + group(channel)
data(channel_sales) + bar * stack + x(col.quarter) + y(col.revenue) + group(col.channel)
data(channel_sales) + bar * stack + x(:quarter) + y(:revenue) +
  group(:channel)
plot(data(channel_sales), layer(bar, stack), x(col.quarter),
  y(col.revenue), group(col.channel))

“Given the channel sales table: bars derived by stack, x is quarter, y is revenue, grouped by channel.”

Each bar’s height is the quarter’s total. Retail comes first in the table, so it is the lower segment of each bar. The thin line marks where the retail revenue ends and the online revenue begins. No color or legend tells the two segments apart. When the reader needs to know which is which, another layer has to label them.

10.11 Stacked bars: piled up

Sometimes the question is the total as well as the parts: how much is there altogether, and how much of it does each group hold? A color split can be placed a second way. Instead of side by side, stack piles the groups on top of each other. Each bar’s height becomes the category’s total across the groups, and the segments read as parts of a whole:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(continent) + y(population) + color(era) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) + color(col.era) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(:continent) + y(:population) +
  color(:era) + y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, sum, stack), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), color(col.era), y_label("Population"),
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by sum and stack, x is continent, y is population, color by era.”

dodge sets the groups side by side, all on one baseline; stack piles them into one bar, whose height is their total. Use stack when the parts add to a meaningful total (populations, counts, revenue), and dodge when you are comparing the groups. The two examples also use different statistics. You stack the sum of population, because quantities add, and you dodge the mean of life, because averages do not.

Grouped bars drew sum where mean was the right statistic, and the opposite works the same way. gog checks that a sentence is well-formed, not that its plot makes sense, and choosing the statistic is your decision (Law 8). Write mean in place of sum, and gog draws it, piling two averages into a bar that reads as their total:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * stack + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy, stacked") +
  title("Mean in place of sum: legal, and meaningless")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * stack + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy, stacked") +
  title("Mean in place of sum: legal, and meaningless"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * stack + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + y_label("Mean life expectancy, stacked") +
  title("Mean in place of sum: legal, and meaningless")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, stack), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), y_label("Mean life expectancy, stacked"),
  title("Mean in place of sum: legal, and meaningless"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and stack, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”

Oceania’s pile reaches about 151 years. A stack reads as parts of a total, so it makes sense only when its values add up, as populations do.

To print each segment’s value inside it, add a text layer with the same stack and a split of its own (Labels on stacked bars).

10.11.1 The 100% stacked bar

The population stack answers two questions at once: how large each total is, and how it splits. The totals differ so much that the small continents’ splits are hard to read. Asia’s 1957 and 2007 populations add up to 5.4 billion, and Oceania’s add up to 0.04 billion. The axis is scaled for Asia, so Oceania’s bar is too short to show its split at all. When the split is the question and the total is not, ask for shares. stack(share = TRUE) divides each segment by its own bar’s total. Each segment then shows its group’s share of the bar, a number from 0 to 1. Every bar reaches 1, so all the splits are on one scale and can be compared across continents:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + x(continent) + y(population) +
  color(era) + title("Each continent's 1957/2007 split, filled to one")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack(share = True) + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
  color(col.era) + title("Each continent's 1957/2007 split, filled to one"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack(share = true) + x(:continent) +
  y(:population) + color(:era) +
  title("Each continent's 1957/2007 split, filled to one")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, sum, stack({ share: true })),
  x(col.continent), y(col.population), color(col.era),
  title("Each continent's 1957/2007 split, filled to one"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by sum and stack as shares, x is continent, y is population, color by era.”

With every bar at 1, the question changes. The population stack compared the two eras inside one continent, and only for the large ones. This plot compares the splits across continents: which population grew the most between the two eras. Africa’s population grew the most. Of its two-era total, 78% falls in 2007 and 22% in 1957, so it more than tripled. Europe’s grew the least: 57% of its total falls in 2007, the closest any continent comes to an even split. Neither number can be read from the population stack above. This plot does not show the totals at all, which is why Oceania’s bar is now as tall as Asia’s. Each plot answers one of the two questions. stack says how much each continent has, and stack(share = TRUE) says how it splits. When you need both answers, draw both plots.

The axis is labeled Share rather than Population, because every value is now a fraction of its bar’s total. Share alone does not say a share of what, so name it yourself with y_label("Share of two-era population"). stack(share = TRUE) is not proportion under another name. The two divide by different totals. proportion divides by the whole plot’s total, so its bars still show how large each category is. This one divides by the bar’s own total.
