stack(share = TRUE) works the same way on a histogram of gapminder_2007, the table shown in Ordering bars. bin cuts the axis into bins, and each segment is then divided by its own bin’s total. The question changes from how many countries fall in each bin to which continents those countries are in:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) * stack(share = TRUE) + x(life) +
  color(continent) + x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  y_label("Share of the countries in the bin") +
  title("Each continent's share of each five-year bin, 2007")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) * stack(share = True) + x(col.life) +
  color(col.continent) + x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  y_label("Share of the countries in the bin") +
  title("Each continent's share of each five-year bin, 2007"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) * stack(share = true) +
  x(:life) + color(:continent) + x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  y_label("Share of the countries in the bin") +
  title("Each continent's share of each five-year bin, 2007")
plot(data(gapminder_2007),
  layer(bar, bin({ width: 5 }), stack({ share: true })), x(col.life),
  color(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  y_label("Share of the countries in the bin"),
  title("Each continent's share of each five-year bin, 2007"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin at width 5 and stack as shares, x is life, color by continent.”

Below 60 years, more than 80% of the countries in each bin are in Africa. From 60 to 70, Asia has the largest share, and Africa and the Americas hold the rest. Europe first appears in the bin from 70 to 75. From 75 to 85, about half of the countries in each bin are European. Oceania’s two countries both fall in the last bin.

This plot hides what the five-year histogram in Histogram shows: how many countries each bin holds. The bin from 35 to 40 holds one country and the bin from 70 to 75 holds 39, but both bars reach 1. When the counts matter, draw that histogram beside this one. In ggplot2, stack(share = TRUE) is written position = "fill". Its five-year bins have other edges, so its bars differ (Where the bin edges fall).

10.11.2 A funnel: bars centered on zero

A funnel shows how many people are left at each stage of a process, from website visits down to invoices sent. Its usual picture is one bar per stage, one above the other, each centered on the same line. The sales_funnel table holds the number of people, in thousands, who reached each stage from each of two sources:

sales_funnel: first 5 of 10 rows
stage source n
Website visit Search 24.0
Downloads Search 16.4
Potential customers Search 12.1
Requested price Search 6.2
Invoice sent Search 1.1

Start with a plain bar chart. The stages go on y, so the bars lie across the page, as in Horizontal bars, and sum adds the two sources of each stage into one bar:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum + y(stage) + x(n) +
  y_label("Stage") + title("One bar per stage, from zero")
(data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum + y(col.stage) + x(col.n) +
  y_label("Stage") + title("One bar per stage, from zero"))
data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum + y(:stage) + x(:n) + y_label("Stage") +
  title("One bar per stage, from zero")
plot(data(sales_funnel), layer(bar, sum), y(col.stage), x(col.n),
  y_label("Stage"), title("One bar per stage, from zero"))

“Given the sales funnel: bars derived by sum, y is stage, x is n.”

Every bar starts at zero, on the left. A funnel moves each bar so that its middle is on one line, and in gog the word that decides where a bar is placed is stack. stack alone is refused here. On its default baseline a pile starts at zero, where these bars already are, and with one bar per stage there is nothing to pile:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack + y(stage) + x(n)
data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack + y(col.stage) + x(col.n)
data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack + y(:stage) + x(:n)
plot(data(sales_funnel), layer(bar, sum, stack), y(col.stage), x(col.n))
Error:
! gog: `bar * stack` has no groups to pile up — nothing splits the mark. Add `color(<field>)` (or `group(<field>)`) so there are groups to stack. To center each pile of one on zero instead, write `stack(baseline = "center")`, which is how a funnel is drawn.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

stack(baseline = "center"), which the message also offers, is the one placement that moves even a pile of one bar: it hangs each bar so that its middle is at zero (Transforms). A text layer with the same transforms writes each total at its bar’s middle (Labels on stacked bars):

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(sales_funnel) + y(stage) + x(n) +
  bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") +
  text * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + label(n) +
  y_label("Stage") + title("A funnel: each stage centered on zero")
(data(sales_funnel) + y(col.stage) + x(col.n) +
  bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") +
  text * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + label(col.n) +
  y_label("Stage") + title("A funnel: each stage centered on zero"))
data(sales_funnel) + y(:stage) + x(:n) +
  bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") +
  text * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + label(:n) + y_label("Stage") +
  title("A funnel: each stage centered on zero")
plot(data(sales_funnel), y(col.stage), x(col.n),
  layer(bar, sum, stack({ baseline: "center" })),
  layer(text, sum, stack({ baseline: "center" })), label(col.n),
  y_label("Stage"), title("A funnel: each stage centered on zero"))

“Given the sales funnel: y is stage, x is n, bars derived by sum and stack on the center baseline, and also text derived by sum and stack on the center baseline, label by n.”

Read it from the top: 39 thousand people visited the website, and 2 thousand were sent an invoice, about one in twenty. The x axis has no numbers, because once a bar has moved off zero, its two ends record only where it was placed. Each label carries its bar’s value instead.

The space between the stages is the bar’s own setting, style(gap = ), the share of each slot left empty (The gap beside each bar). Here is the funnel at the default gap, 0.2, then at 0.05 and at 0. The first plot is given more width with theme(width = ), because it alone carries the stage names, so the three panels come out the same size:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(stage) + x(n) +
   style(gap = 0.2) + y_label("Stage") + title("gap = 0.2") + theme(width = 400)) |
  (data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(stage) + x(n) +
     style(gap = 0.05) + title("gap = 0.05") + theme(width = 240)) |
  (data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(stage) + x(n) +
     style(gap = 0) + title("gap = 0") + theme(width = 240))
((data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(col.stage) + x(col.n) +
   style(gap = 0.2) + y_label("Stage") + title("gap = 0.2") + theme(width = 400)) |
  (data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(col.stage) + x(col.n) +
     style(gap = 0.05) + title("gap = 0.05") + theme(width = 240)) |
  (data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(col.stage) + x(col.n) +
     style(gap = 0) + title("gap = 0") + theme(width = 240)))
(data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(:stage) +
  x(:n) + style(gap = 0.2) + y_label("Stage") + title("gap = 0.2") +
  theme(width = 400)) |
  (data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") +
  y(:stage) + x(:n) + style(gap = 0.05) + title("gap = 0.05") +
  theme(width = 240)) |
  (data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") +
  y(:stage) + x(:n) + style(gap = 0) + title("gap = 0") +
  theme(width = 240))
beside(beside(plot(data(sales_funnel),
  layer(bar, sum, stack({ baseline: "center" })), y(col.stage), x(col.n),
  style({ gap: 0.2 }), y_label("Stage"), title("gap = 0.2"),
  theme({ width: 400 })),
  plot(data(sales_funnel), layer(bar, sum, stack({ baseline: "center" })),
  y(col.stage), x(col.n), style({ gap: 0.05 }), title("gap = 0.05"),
  theme({ width: 240 }))),
  plot(data(sales_funnel), layer(bar, sum, stack({ baseline: "center" })),
  y(col.stage), x(col.n), style({ gap: 0 }), title("gap = 0"),
  theme({ width: 240 })))

“Given the sales funnel: bars derived by sum and stack on the center baseline, y is stage, x is n, with gap 0.2, beside the same with gap 0.05, beside the same with gap 0.”

At 0.2 each stage is apart from the next. At 0.05 the stages nearly touch, and the bars read as one funnel. At 0 they touch, and only the steps at each bar’s ends show where one stage ends and the next begins.

No atom in the sentence is a funnel. With no split, stack piles nothing and only places each bar. Split the bars by a group, and it does both: it piles the groups end to end and centers the pile. Write color(source) after the bar, here with the gap at 0.05:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(stage) + x(n) +
  color(source) + style(gap = 0.05) +
  y_label("Stage") + title("The same funnel, split by source")
(data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(col.stage) + x(col.n) +
  color(col.source) + style(gap = 0.05) +
  y_label("Stage") + title("The same funnel, split by source"))
data(sales_funnel) + bar * sum * stack(baseline = "center") + y(:stage) +
  x(:n) + color(:source) + style(gap = 0.05) + y_label("Stage") +
  title("The same funnel, split by source")
plot(data(sales_funnel), layer(bar, sum, stack({ baseline: "center" })),
  y(col.stage), x(col.n), color(col.source), style({ gap: 0.05 }),
  y_label("Stage"), title("The same funnel, split by source"))

“Given the sales funnel: bars derived by sum and stack on the center baseline, y is stage, x is n, color by source.”

Search, the blue segments, brought 24 of the 39 thousand visits, and Referral, the orange ones, brought 15. The two shrink at different rates. By the invoices they are almost even, 1.1 thousand from Search and 0.9 from Referral. This plot has no labels, because the last stage’s two segments are narrower than their numbers. The table above holds them. gog draws no sloped connectors between the stages, because the space between two categories holds no data.

10.12 Grouped, stacked or 100% stacked?

You have now seen three ways to place a color split. dodge sets the groups side by side, stack piles them up, and stack(share = TRUE) piles them up as shares. Each way makes one question easy to answer and another question hard, so the choice depends on the question your reader must answer. To see the difference, draw one table all three ways.

The titanic table counts the people aboard the Titanic, the ship that sank in 1912. Each row is one combination of class, sex, age and survived, and n says how many people match it, sometimes none. Each row already holds a count, so the plots add up n with sum rather than counting rows with count. color(survived) then splits each class into the people who survived and the people who died.

One legend explains all three plots below, so legend = FALSE leaves it out of the first two. The third plot asks for 330 pixels of the arrangement’s width with theme(width = 330), so its legend has room.

titanic: first 5 of 32 rows
class sex age survived n
1st Male Adult Yes 57
1st Male Adult No 118
1st Male Child Yes 5
1st Male Child No 0
1st Female Adult Yes 140
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
((data(titanic) + bar * sum * dodge + x(class) + y(n) +
    color(survived, legend = FALSE) + y_label("People") + title("dodge")) |
  (data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(class) + y(n) +
    color(survived, legend = FALSE) + title("stack")) |
  (data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + x(class) + y(n) +
    color(survived) + y_label("Share of the class") +
    title("stack(share = TRUE)") + theme(width = 330))) +
  theme(height = 360)
(((data(titanic) + bar * sum * dodge + x(col["class"]) + y(col.n) +
    color(col.survived, legend = False) + y_label("People") + title("dodge")) |
  (data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(col["class"]) + y(col.n) +
    color(col.survived, legend = False) + title("stack")) |
  (data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack(share = True) + x(col["class"]) + y(col.n) +
    color(col.survived) + y_label("Share of the class") +
    title("stack(share = TRUE)") + theme(width = 330))) +
  theme(height = 360))
((data(titanic) + bar * sum * dodge + x(:class) + y(:n) +
  color(:survived, legend = false) + y_label("People") + title("dodge")) |
  (data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(:class) + y(:n) +
  color(:survived, legend = false) + title("stack")) |
  (data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack(share = true) + x(:class) + y(:n) +
  color(:survived) + y_label("Share of the class") +
  title("stack(share = TRUE)") + theme(width = 330))) +
  theme(height = 360)
beside(beside(plot(data(titanic), layer(bar, sum, dodge), x(col.class),
  y(col.n), color(col.survived, { legend: false }), y_label("People"),
  title("dodge")),
  plot(data(titanic), layer(bar, sum, stack), x(col.class), y(col.n),
  color(col.survived, { legend: false }), title("stack"))),
  plot(data(titanic), layer(bar, sum, stack({ share: true })),
  x(col.class), y(col.n), color(col.survived),
  y_label("Share of the class"), title("stack(share = TRUE)"),
  theme({ width: 330 })), theme({ height: 360 }))

“Given titanic: bars derived by sum and dodge, x is class, y is n, color by survived, without a legend, beside bars derived by sum and stack, x is class, y is n, color by survived, without a legend, beside bars derived by sum and stack as shares, x is class, y is n, color by survived.”

All three plots start from the same eight sums: the survivors and the dead in each class. The first two read n on the y axis, so they share one axis, drawn once at the left. That axis is sized for the crew’s total, 885, which is why the dodge plot leaves room above its tallest bar, 673. The third plot divides each segment by its class’s total, so it draws a separate axis, from 0 to 1. y_label() names that axis, as in The 100% stacked bar.

Each plot answers one kind of question best, and each one hides something. For each plot, the table gives both:

Plot Answers best Hides
dodge Did more people survive or die in each class? Did more people die in third class or in the crew? Each class’s total. To see it, you must add two bar heights yourself.
stack How many people were in each class, and how many of them survived? How the deaths compare across classes. The segments of the dead start at different heights.
stack(share = TRUE) In which class was a person most likely to survive? How many people each class held. Second class held 285 people and the crew 885, but both bars reach 1.

dodge answers its questions because every bar starts at zero, so any two bars can be compared by height. In the first plot, for example, first class is the only class with more survivors than dead. In stack, only the bottom group, the survivors, starts at zero. stack(share = TRUE) makes every bar reach 1, so each segment’s height is its share of the class.

The crew and first class show why the choice depends on the question. If you count the survivors, as the first two plots do, the two have nearly the same number: 212 against 203. If you divide by each class’s total, as the third plot does, they are far apart: 24% of the crew survived, against 62% of first class. Both facts are true, and each plot shows only one of them. When the reader needs more than one answer, draw more than one plot, as this section does.

10.13 Transforms it takes

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a bar takes and the ones it refuses:

Kind Takes Refuses
Counting bin, count, density, proportion —
Summaries sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile —
Fitted lines smooth, straight —
Running total cumulative —
Pairs: a low and a high — range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band, bounds
Collision modifiers dodge, stack jitter, repel
Layouts of a whole picture — partition, flow, layout, cluster

The plots below show every transform a bar takes. Within a figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any other change.

Counting. count and proportion tally the rows at each value of x, on a category or a number. bin and density work on a number. bin counts the rows in each interval, and density estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely the rows lie along the axis. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty. The top two plots put continent on x, and the plot below them puts life. On a bar, bin gives the histogram:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + title("bar * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
     title("bar * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) + title("bar * bin"))
(((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + title("bar * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent) +
     title("bar * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) + title("bar * bin")))
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  title("bar * count")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent) +
  title("bar * proportion"))) /
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) + title("bar * bin"))
below(beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count),
  x(col.continent), title("bar * count")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent),
  title("bar * proportion"))),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  title("bar * bin")))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, beside bars derived by proportion, x is continent; above bars derived by bin, x is life.”

The density is drawn in a figure of its own. In one figure with the bin plot, the two would share one life axis that covers only the range of the rows, and the density’s tails would be cut off (A plot cut by a shared axis). density gives one bar at each place where the curve was computed, with a gap between neighboring bars, as bars beside a category have. The places run a little past the data on both sides, where the curve is close to zero, so the outermost bars are too short to see. The plots below leave places at its default, 256, and set it to 32:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(life) +
   title("bar * density: 256 places, the default")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density(places = 32) + x(life) +
     title("bar * density(places = 32)"))
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(col.life) +
   title("bar * density: 256 places, the default")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density(places = 32) + x(col.life) +
     title("bar * density(places = 32)")))
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(:life) +
  title("bar * density: 256 places, the default")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density(places = 32) + x(:life) +
  title("bar * density(places = 32)"))
beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, density), x(col.life),
  title("bar * density: 256 places, the default")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, density({ places: 32 })),
  x(col.life), title("bar * density(places = 32)")))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by density, x is life, beside bars derived by density at 32 places, x is life.”

At 256 places the bars touch and form one shape. At 32, the gaps between them can be seen.

Look at the y axis of the five plots above, from bar * count to bar * density(places = 32). None of the five sentences writes y(), yet each y axis has a name: Count, Proportion, Count, Density and Density. The table has no column by those names. Each transform writes one, and y draws it. count and bin write count, the number of rows at each value or in each interval. proportion writes proportion, each count’s share of all the rows. density writes density, the height of the estimated curve. The axis is labeled with the column’s name, capitalized, as The name on a measure axis explains.

Summaries. The six summaries reduce the rows at each value of x to one value, so they need a number on y. Each bar then reaches that value. sum reads population, because only an amount has a total that means something. The other five read life. They give the mean, the median, the largest and the smallest value, and quantile(0.9) gives the value that nine tenths of the rows fall below:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +
    title("bar * sum")) |

below(beside(beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum),
  x(col.continent), y(col.population), title("bar * sum")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), title("bar * mean"))),

  y(col.life), title("bar * median"))),

  x(col.continent), y(col.life), title("bar * max")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, min), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), title("bar * min"))),

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum, x is continent, y is population, beside bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, beside bars derived by median, x is continent, y is life; above bars derived by max, x is continent, y is life, beside bars derived by min, x is continent, y is life, beside bars derived by quantile at 0.9, x is continent, y is life.”

The five plots that read life share one scale, so their heights can be compared from plot to plot. Duplicate categories shows why a bar needs a summary when a table holds several rows for one category.

Fitted lines. smooth and straight need a number on each axis. They fit a line to the rows, each placed at its x and its y. smooth follows the shape of the data, and straight is the least-squares line. A fitted line is usually drawn with line, as a curve or a straight line over the points (Smoothed trend line). gog draws it on a bar as well, which is legal but unusual, as bars at evenly spaced places along x, and their tops trace the line. There are 100 places unless you set places, and the first two plots ask for 24, so that each bar can be seen.

Running total. cumulative adds each value to the ones before it along the axis. After bin, it gives the cumulative histogram, and with start_from = "previous" each bar starts at the total before it, as in the waterfall. The third plot reads the actuals table, with year on x and sales on y. The table holds one year of sales in each row:

actuals: all 5 rows
year sales
2019 120
2020 135
2021 128
2022 152
2023 168
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * smooth(places = 24) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
   title("bar * smooth(places = 24)")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * straight(places = 24) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
     title("bar * straight(places = 24)")) |
  (data(actuals) + bar * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
     title("bar * cumulative"))
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * smooth(places = 24) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
   title("bar * smooth(places = 24)")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * straight(places = 24) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
     title("bar * straight(places = 24)")) |
  (data(actuals) + bar * cumulative + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
     title("bar * cumulative")))
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * smooth(places = 24) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  title("bar * smooth(places = 24)")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * straight(places = 24) + x(:gdp) +
  y(:life) + title("bar * straight(places = 24)")) |
  (data(actuals) + bar * cumulative + x(:year) + y(:sales) +
  title("bar * cumulative"))
beside(beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007),
  layer(bar, smooth({ places: 24 })), x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  title("bar * smooth(places = 24)")),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, straight({ places: 24 })),
  x(col.gdp), y(col.life), title("bar * straight(places = 24)"))),
  plot(data(actuals), layer(bar, cumulative), x(col.year), y(col.sales),
  title("bar * cumulative")))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by smooth at 24 places, x is gdp, y is life, beside bars derived by straight at 24 places, x is gdp, y is life; beside bars from the actuals, derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales.”

Collision modifiers. Collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another. On a bar they place the bars that would share one slot. dodge sets them side by side, and stack piles them up. stack(share = TRUE) also piles them up, and divides each piece by its bar’s total. All three need the rows split by color, pattern or group, so that each slot holds more than one bar. The gm_eras table, shown in Horizontal bars, holds one row for each country in each era, so each plot also needs a summary before the modifier. The dodge plot averages life. The two stacks add up population, because only an amount has a total that means something:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
     title("bar * mean * dodge")) |
    (data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(continent) + y(population) +
       color(era) + title("bar * sum * stack"))) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + x(continent) +
      y(population) + color(era) + title("bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE)"))) +
  theme(height = 800)
((((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
     title("bar * mean * dodge")) |
    (data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
       color(col.era) + title("bar * sum * stack"))) /
   (data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack(share = True) + x(col.continent) +
      y(col.population) + color(col.era) + title("bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE)"))) +
  theme(height = 800))
(((data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + title("bar * mean * dodge")) |
  (data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(:continent) + y(:population) +
  color(:era) + title("bar * sum * stack"))) /
  (data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack(share = true) + x(:continent) +
  y(:population) + color(:era) +
  title("bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE)"))) + theme(height = 800)
below(beside(plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge),
  x(col.continent), y(col.life), color(col.era),
  title("bar * mean * dodge")),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, sum, stack), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), color(col.era), title("bar * sum * stack"))),
  plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, sum, stack({ share: true })),
  x(col.continent), y(col.population), color(col.era),
  title("bar * sum * stack(share = TRUE)")), theme({ height: 800 }))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era, beside bars derived by sum and stack, x is continent, y is population, color by era; above bars derived by sum and stack as shares, x is continent, y is population, color by era.”

Grouped bars and Stacked bars explain each one in full.

A bar refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. The pair transforms give y a low and a high at each value of x, which interval, ribbon, line and step take. jitter moves each point a short way along the categorical axis, and only point takes it. repel moves text labels off each other. partition, flow and cluster lay out rectangles, bands and branches, which zone, ribbon and path draw. layout places a network, which point, text and edge draw.

10.14 What you can set

A setting changes how every bar looks without reading a column, and each mark takes its own. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a bar’s settings, with the values each accepts:

Setting Value
style(color = ) any CSS color name or hex
style(opacity = ) 0 to 1
style(pattern = ) solid, hatch, crosshatch, stripes, grid, dots
style(border_color = ) any CSS color name or hex
style(border_size = ) pixels
style(gap = ) a share of the mark’s place, from 0 to just under 1

A bar has no size, and that is deliberate. Its value sets its length, and its slot sets its width, so a size in pixels would be a second, conflicting width. gap does not conflict, because it is a share of the slot: it sets how much of the slot the bar leaves empty (The gap beside each bar). A bar is a shape with an inside and an outline, so it does have a border.

A fill, a texture and a border compose, so one layer can carry all three. The plot uses the medals table, shown in Basic usage:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
  style(color = "goldenrod", pattern = "crosshatch",
        border_color = "black", border_size = 1) +
  y_label("Gold medals") + title("A fill, a texture, and a border")
(data(medals) + bar * sum + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  style(color = "goldenrod", pattern = "crosshatch",
        border_color = "black", border_size = 1) +
  y_label("Gold medals") + title("A fill, a texture, and a border"))
data(medals) + bar * sum + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  style(color = "goldenrod", pattern = "crosshatch", border_color = "black", border_size = 1) +
  y_label("Gold medals") + title("A fill, a texture, and a border")
plot(data(medals), layer(bar, sum), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  style({ color: "goldenrod", pattern: "crosshatch",
  border_color: "black", border_size: 1 }), y_label("Gold medals"),
  title("A fill, a texture, and a border"))

“Given the medals: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold, colored goldenrod, with pattern crosshatch, border color black and border size 1.”

The settings table above lists the six fill textures a bar takes. A line takes five stroke patterns instead, and only "solid" is in both lists.

The histogram’s bins are not a setting. bin(30) and bin(width = 5) belong to the transform, because they change what is counted, not how a bar is drawn. Histogram shows bin(width = 5), and Choosing the bin count shows both.

The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

10.15 What it refuses

The five refusals below have different causes. The first two belong to the transform rather than the mark: bin needs a continuous axis to cut, and count computes the number it draws. The other three belong to the mark: a bar is a fill rather than a stroke, a bar needs a number to measure, and on a bar with no transform, splitting by group would change nothing.

Binning cuts a continuous axis into intervals, so there is nothing for it to cut on a categorical one:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(continent)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.continent)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:continent)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.continent))
Error:
! gog: `bin` cuts a continuous axis into intervals, and `x(continent)` is categorical — a category is one slot, with no width to cut. To tally rows per category, `count` is the transform that does it: `bar * count`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

To count the rows in each category’s slot, use count. The refusal names bar * count rather than drawing empty bins.

The second refusal comes from count itself. On y, count draws the number of rows in each slot, so a column named on y would never be read. gog refuses it, because the axis would be titled life while its numbers are counts:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + y(life)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) + y(:life)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `bar * count` counts the rows in each slot, and draws that number on `y`, so `y(life)` names a column it never reads: the axis would be titled `life` over numbers that are not `life`. To summarize `life` in each slot instead of counting rows, name a statistic that reads it, such as `bar * mean`. To title the axis, write `y_label()`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

To summarize life in each slot, use a statistic that reads it, such as bar * mean. y(count) in the first histogram is accepted, because it names the column that bin writes.

The third refusal is about texture. A bar is a filled shape, so it takes the fill textures, such as "hatch". "dashed" is a stroke pattern:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(gold) + style(pattern = "dashed")
data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + style(pattern = "dashed")
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:gold) + style(pattern = "dashed")
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  style({ pattern: "dashed" }))
Error:
! gog: `style(pattern = )` on a `bar`: `"dashed"` is a stroke pattern, not a fill texture. Use "solid" (the default), "hatch", "crosshatch", "stripes", "grid", "dots".
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

A bar’s outline takes a color and a width, never a stroke pattern. border_color and border_size are the only two settings the outline has.

Two categorical positions are the fourth refusal. The axis with the category places the bars, one slot each, and the axis with the number measures how far they reach, as Horizontal bars explained. With a category on both, there is no length left to draw:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + x(country) + y(country)
data(medals) + bar + x(col.country) + y(col.country)
data(medals) + bar + x(:country) + y(:country)
plot(data(medals), bar, x(col.country), y(col.country))
Error:
! gog: `bar` has categorical columns on both axes — `x(country)` and `y(country)` — so there is nothing for it to measure. One axis must hold a continuous column: that is the length of the bar. To count the rows instead, `bar * count + x(country)` draws one bar for each `country`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The message names two fixes: put a number on one axis, or count the rows per category with bar * count.

The fifth refusal is group on a bar with no transform. Each row of the table is already its own bar, so splitting the rows by era would change nothing in the picture. The plot titled bar: one bar per row, in Splitting without color, shows that picture. With group(era) added, gog refuses the sentence:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar + x(continent) + y(life) + group(era)
data(gm_eras) + bar + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + group(col.era)
data(gm_eras) + bar + x(:continent) + y(:life) + group(:era)
plot(data(gm_eras), bar, x(col.continent), y(col.life), group(col.era))
Error:
! gog: `group` on a `bar` needs `dodge`, `stack` or a statistic to act on. Each row is already its own bar, so splitting the rows by `era` alone would change nothing. Add `dodge` to set the bars of each `era` side by side, as in `bar * dodge`, or add a statistic such as `mean` when a slot holds several rows of one `era`, as in `bar * mean * dodge`. Or map `era` to `color`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The message names three fixes. The first, dodge, sets the two eras’ bars side by side in each slot. It is enough when the table holds one row for each bar, as channel_sales does. gm_eras holds one row for each country, so it needs the second fix as well: a statistic such as mean, as in Splitting without color. The third fix writes color(era) in place of group(era), which gives each era its own color and a legend. On this table it still needs mean * dodge to draw one bar for each era.

10.16 In short

The axis with the category places the bars, and the axis with the number measures them. A bar’s length is its value, and that axis reaches zero unless you state your own limits. Without a transform one bar is drawn per row, and rows sharing a category overlap in one slot. A categorical bar fills 80% of its slot unless you set gap. A histogram bar fills its whole bin, and bin() decides how wide a bin is.

10.17 What comes next

The gap on each side of a bar says that the categories are separate. When the positions are continuous, such as the years of a sales series, the area mark (Area) joins each value to the next and fills the region below them, with no gaps.
